SK6034 A public constant is baked into every caller

The compiler copies a const into the consuming assembly, so changing it and shipping only your own assembly leaves every caller on the old value with no error anywhere.

CategoryDesign
Default severitysuggestion
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno

Fixyes, review it

Since2.0
SupersedesS2339

Why

⚠ This is a property of how the value is distributed, not of how the declaration is written. The compiler does not emit a field read for Limits.MaxRetries; it emits the literal 3, into the consumer's assembly. Ship version 2 of the library with the value changed to 5, and every assembly that was built against version 1 keeps 3 — the load succeeds, no binding redirect fires, no analyzer complains, and the two halves of the program disagree about a number they both believe they read from one place. It is the one versioning hazard in .NET with no diagnostic at all behind it: a renamed member is a MissingMethodException, a changed signature is a MissingMethodException, and a changed constant is silence. static readonly is read from the field at run time and does not have this property, at the cost of one indirection and a type initializer. The reason to keep a const public is that its value is part of the contract and can never change — a protocol magic number, a format version, a mathematical constant — and that is a claim worth making on purpose rather than by default. ⚠ `dotnet_code_quality.SK6034.frozen_constant_types` is where that claim is made. It names the containing types whose constants are contract, it defaults to empty — so the rule reports everything until a project says otherwise — and the analyzer holds no opinion about which names are special.

Example

Instead of:

public static class Limits {
    public const int MaxRetries = 3;
}

Write:

public static class Limits {
    public static readonly int MaxRetries = 3;
}

When it does not fire

⚠ A project declares which of its constants are frozen; the analyzer never guesses. dotnet_code_quality.SK6034.frozen_constant_types takes a comma-separated list of containing type names — either the simple name or the fully qualified one — and every const in a named type is exempt. It defaults to empty, so nothing is exempt until the project says so, which is the "on purpose rather than by default" the rationale asks for. ⚠ The key takes type names and not values, and an earlier proposal that keyed the exemption on this repository's own `allocated-ids.txt` and on the type names `RuleIds`/`ExitCodes` was withdrawn as exactly the calibration this project forbids — the rule ships to codebases that have none of those. ⚠ Skala itself does not set the key, and cannot — its root .editorconfig is root = true plus the ReSharper export byte for byte (ADR-015, asserted by EditorConfigIngestionTests), its digest is what 2 814 conformance fixtures record as the configuration they were frozen under, and ChainWalk_StopsAtRoot asserts there is no nested one. Measured with the key set anyway, SK6034 falls from 162 findings on this tree to 108, and the 54 that go are ArrangeIds, ConfigDiagnosticIds, ExitCodes and FormatDiagnosticIds.

⚠ The rule cannot tell a value that will never change from one that is merely constant today, and that is the whole false-positive story. A protocol magic number, a wire format version, "\r\n", a mathematical constant and a spec-mandated field width are all correctly public const: the value is part of the contract, so a caller holding the old copy holds the right one. A retry count, a buffer size, a timeout, a URL and a display string are the opposite, and nothing in the declaration separates the two. The rule ships at suggestion for this reason, and the answer for a value that really is fixed is a suppression with the sentence saying why.

⚠ The harm needs an assembly boundary, and the rule cannot see whether there is one. In a solution rebuilt end to end on every commit, const is fine — everything is recompiled, so every copy is refreshed at once. The hazard is real for a library that ships independently of its consumers, which is the general case and the one the rule assumes. An application with no reference surface is where a suppression is cheapest.

`internal` and `private` constants are never reported, and neither is a `public const` inside an `internal` type. Visibility is computed by walking the field's accessibility and every containing type's, because a public const that cannot leave the assembly is never copied anywhere compiled separately. That walk is the difference between this rule and one that reports every public const in a program. InternalsVisibleTo does not change the answer: the friend assembly is in the same solution and rebuilt with it.

Constants in an interface are excluded. A static readonly field in an interface is legal and is not the same declaration — it changes what implementers see and when the runtime initializes it — so the one-token fix would not be the repair it claims to be.

⚠ The fix drops an initialiser that is already the type's default, because keeping it is `CA1805`. public const int Ok = 0; swapped to public static readonly int Ok = 0; is an explicit default initialiser — redundant on a field, legitimate on a const — so the one-token edit traded this rule's finding for the SDK's. Only value types are dropped: const string X = null; would become an uninitialised non-nullable field, which is CS8618 and a worse trade than the one being repaired.

⚠ The fix is `fixIsSafe: false`, and the breakage it can cause lands in files the edit does not touch. A const is usable where the language demands a compile-time constant and a static readonly field is not: an attribute argument (CS0182), an optional parameter's default value (CS1736), a case label or constant pattern (CS0150), another const's initializer (CS0133), and goto case. Every one of those is a compiler error rather than a silent behaviour change, so the edit is never dangerous — but each is a caller's build, possibly in another repository, and "apply without review" is a promise this rule cannot make. Two smaller consequences go with it: the value stops being folded at compile time, so a comparison against it is no longer a constant expression; and the type gains a static initializer where it may have had none.

⚠ There is deliberately no local guard against those positions. The rule could refuse to report a const that the same file uses in an attribute argument or a parameter default, and it does not — because the identical breakage across an assembly boundary is precisely what this rule exists to say it cannot see, and a guard that catches only the visible half would make the finding look better checked than it is. fixIsSafe: false is the honest statement, and it is one statement rather than two.

One finding per declaration, not per declarator. public const int A = 1, B = 2; has one const token and one edit; two findings would carry the same replacement twice. A declaration whose const token carries a preprocessor directive is skipped, for the reason SK6003 skips one: the token the fix names may not be the token every branch compiles.
